title: How Mountains Grow
summary: How moving plates fold rock into mountains, how lava builds volcanoes, and how erosion slowly wears mountains down.

versions.title: Rocks That Rise
versions.text:
Look at a tall hill of rock. It is a mountain. How did it get so big?

The ground is like a hard shell. The shell is the crust. It is cut up in big parts. The parts are plates. The plates move. They move as slow as your nails grow.

Two plates can push hard on each other. Then the rock bends. It folds up, like a rug that you push on the floor. Each year it goes up a bit more. Big peaks rise. That is how Mount Everest grew. It is the top peak in the world.

Some peaks grow in a new way. Hot rock comes up. It is lava. It cools and gets hard. Then more lava comes. Bit by bit, it makes a volcano.

Rain, wind, and ice wear the rock down. So peaks grow, and they shrink, too.

Saudi Arabia has peaks by the Red Sea. They rose as the land there split and slid away.

versions.title: Rocks That Rise
versions.text:
Have you seen a tall mountain? How did it get so big?

The ground is like a hard shell. The shell is called the crust. It is cut up in huge parts. They are called plates. The plates move all the time. They move as slow as your nails grow.

Sometimes two plates push on each other. Then the rock bends and folds up. It is like a rug that you push on the floor. Each year it goes up a bit more. In time, tall peaks rise. That is how Mount Everest grew. It is the top peak in the world.

Some mountains grow in a new way. Hot, melted rock comes up from deep down. It is called lava. It cools and gets hard. Then more lava comes on top. Bit by bit, it builds a volcano.

Rain, wind, and ice wear the rock down. So mountains grow, but they also shrink.

Saudi Arabia has a long line of mountains by the Red Sea. They rose as the land there split and slid away.

versions.title: How Mountains Grow
versions.text:
Some mountains are so tall that snow sits on top all year. But how does a mountain get so big?

The ground we stand on is like a hard shell. This shell is called the crust. It is broken into giant pieces called plates. The plates move all the time. They move about as fast as your fingernails grow.

Sometimes two plates push into each other. When that happens, the rock bends and folds up. Think of a rug that you push across the floor. It bunches up in the middle. Over millions of years, the folds rise into tall mountains. That is how Mount Everest was made. It is the tallest mountain in the world, and it is still growing.

Other mountains grow in a different way. Hot, melted rock comes up from deep below. It is called lava. The lava cools and turns hard. Then more lava flows on top. Layer by layer, it builds a volcano.

Rain, wind, and ice slowly break rock down. So mountains grow, but they also shrink.

In Saudi Arabia, a long line of mountains runs beside the Red Sea. They rose as the land there split apart.

versions.title: How Mountains Grow
versions.text:
Some mountains are so tall that their tops are covered in snow all year. But mountains were not always that tall. So how does a mountain grow?

The ground under our feet is like the hard shell of an egg. This shell is called the crust. It is cracked into giant pieces called plates. The plates are always moving, but very slowly. They move about as fast as your fingernails grow.

Sometimes two plates push against each other. When that happens, the rock bends and folds upward. Think of pushing a rug across the floor until it bunches up. Over millions of years, these folds rise into tall mountains. Mount Everest formed this way when two plates crashed together. It is the tallest mountain on Earth, and it is still growing a tiny bit each year.

Other mountains grow in a different way. Hot, melted rock rises from deep underground. When it pours out, it is called lava. The lava cools and hardens into rock. Then more lava flows on top. Layer by layer, it builds a volcano.

At the same time, rain, wind, and ice slowly break rock apart. So mountains grow, but they also wear down.

In Saudi Arabia, a long line of mountains runs beside the Red Sea. They rose as the land there slowly split apart.

versions.title: How Mountains Grow
versions.text:
Some mountains are so tall that their tops stay covered in snow all year. Yet mountains were not always that tall. Like living things, they grow, and they also get worn down.

The ground under our feet is like the hard shell of an egg. This shell is called the crust, and it is cracked into giant pieces called plates. The plates are always moving, but very slowly. They move only a few centimeters a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.

Sometimes two plates collide. When that happens, the rock between them bends and folds upward. Think of pushing a rug across the floor until it bunches up. Over millions of years, these folds rise into tall mountains. Mount Everest formed this way when the plate carrying India crashed into Asia. Its summit is the highest point on Earth, and it is still rising a few millimeters each year. Climbers have even found fossils of sea animals near the top, which shows that this rock was once under the sea.

Other mountains grow in a different way. Deep underground, rock is so hot that it melts. This melted rock is called magma. When it pours out at the surface, it is called lava. The lava cools and hardens, and then more lava flows on top. Layer by layer, a volcano grows.

Meanwhile, rain, wind, and ice slowly break rock apart and carry it away. This is called erosion. So mountains grow, but they also wear down.

In Saudi Arabia, the Sarawat Mountains run beside the Red Sea. They rose as the land there slowly split away from Africa.

versions.text:

versions.title: How Mountains Grow
versions.text:
Some mountains are so tall that their peaks remain covered in snow throughout the year, yet mountains were not always that tall. In some ways, they behave like living things, because they grow over very long periods of time while also being gradually worn down.

The ground beneath our feet is like the hard shell of an egg, and this shell, called the crust, is cracked into giant pieces called tectonic plates, which are constantly moving, although very slowly, traveling only a few centimeters each year, which is roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.

Sometimes two plates collide, and when that happens, the force can compress the rock between them so that it bends and folds upward, much like a rug that bunches up when you push it across a smooth floor. Over millions of years, this uplift raises enormous mountain ranges. Mount Everest formed this way when the plate carrying India crashed into Asia, and its summit, the highest point on Earth, is still rising a few millimeters every year. Climbers have even discovered fossils of sea creatures near the top, which proves that this rock began as sediment at the bottom of an ancient sea.

Other mountains grow in a completely different way. Deep underground, rock becomes so hot that it melts into magma, and when this magma erupts at the surface, it is called lava. The lava cools and hardens, and then more lava flows on top of it, so that layer by layer a volcano gradually grows taller.

Meanwhile, rain, wind, and ice slowly break rock apart and carry the pieces away in a process called erosion. As a result, mountains are growing and wearing down at the same time.

In Saudi Arabia, the Sarawat Mountains stretch along the Red Sea coast. They were lifted up along a rift as the Arabian Plate slowly pulled away from Africa, which opened up the sea between the two continents. The highest of these peaks, Jabal Sawda near the city of Abha, rises about three thousand meters above sea level, which is high enough that its air stays cool even when the lowlands below are very hot.

versions.title: How Mountains Grow
versions.text:
Some mountains are so tall that their peaks remain covered in snow throughout the year, yet mountains were not always so impressive. In certain ways, they resemble living things, because they grow over extremely long periods of time while simultaneously being gradually worn down.

The ground beneath our feet resembles the hard shell of an egg, and this shell, called the crust, is fractured into gigantic sections called tectonic plates, which are continuously moving, although very slowly, traveling only a few centimeters annually, which is approximately the speed at which your fingernails grow.

Occasionally two plates collide, and when that happens, the tremendous force can compress the rock between them so that it bends and folds upward, much like a rug that bunches up when you push it across a smooth floor. Climbers have even discovered fossils of marine creatures near the top, which demonstrates that this rock originally formed from sediment at the bottom of an ancient ocean.

Other mountains develop in an entirely different manner. Deep underground, rock becomes so hot that it melts into magma, and when this magma erupts at the surface, it is called lava. The lava cools and solidifies, and then additional lava flows on top of it, so that layer by layer a volcano gradually grows taller.

Meanwhile, rain, wind, and ice steadily break rock apart and transport the fragments away in a process called erosion, and consequently, mountains are growing and wearing down simultaneously.

versions.title: How Mountains Grow
versions.text:
Some mountains are so tall that their peaks remain covered in snow throughout the year, yet mountains were not always so impressive. In certain respects, they resemble living organisms, because they develop over extraordinarily long periods of time while simultaneously being gradually worn down.

The ground beneath our feet resembles the brittle shell of an egg, and this shell, called the crust, is fractured into gigantic sections called tectonic plates, which are continuously moving, although extremely slowly, traveling only a few centimeters annually, which is approximately the speed at which your fingernails grow.

Occasionally two plates collide, and when that happens, the tremendous pressure can compress the rock between them so that it buckles and folds upward, much like a rug that bunches up when you push it across a polished floor. Over millions of years, this gradual uplift produces enormous mountain ranges. Mount Everest originated this way when the plate carrying India collided with Asia, and its summit, the highest elevation on Earth, is still rising a few millimeters every year. Geologists estimate that this collision began approximately fifty million years ago, and because the plates continue to press together, the Himalayas have not yet stopped growing. Climbers have even discovered fossils of marine creatures near the top, which demonstrates that this rock originally formed from sediment deposited at the bottom of an ancient ocean.

Other mountains develop in an entirely different manner. Deep underground, rock becomes so intensely hot that it melts into magma, and when this magma erupts at the surface, it is called lava. The lava cools and solidifies, and then additional lava accumulates on top of it, so that layer by layer a volcano gradually becomes taller.

Meanwhile, rain, wind, and ice steadily break rock apart and transport the fragments elsewhere in a process called erosion, and consequently, mountains are simultaneously growing and deteriorating.

In Saudi Arabia, the Sarawat Mountains extend along the Red Sea coast, and they were elevated along a rift as the Arabian Plate gradually separated from Africa, a geological process that also created the sea between the two continents. The highest of these peaks, Jabal Sawda near the city of Abha, rises approximately three thousand meters above sea level, an elevation sufficient to keep its atmosphere cool and frequently foggy even when the surrounding lowlands experience intense summer temperatures.

keyWords.definition: the hard outside layer of the Earth
keyWords.example: We live on the crust, the thin rocky skin of our planet.

keyWords.definition: huge pieces of the Earth's crust that slowly move
keyWords.example: Scientists track how the plates under the ocean shift each year.

keyWords.definition: to bend something so one part rises or lies over another
keyWords.example: Please fold the paper in half before you write on it.

keyWords.definition: a mountain built by hot melted rock that comes up from inside the Earth
keyWords.example: Smoke rose from the top of the volcano in the photo.

keyWords.definition: hot melted rock that flows out onto the ground
keyWords.example: The black rock near the hill was once red-hot lava.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to climb a tall mountain safely
The ways mountains grow and wear down
Why snow falls on mountain tops
Which animals live on mountains
questions.why: The article explains how moving plates and lava make mountains grow, and how rain, wind, and ice wear them down.

wrong.A: The article does not teach how to climb.
wrong.C: Snow is mentioned, but the article does not explain why it falls.
wrong.D: The article does not talk about mountain animals.

questions.stem: How fast do the Earth's plates move?
options: As fast as a car on a road
As fast as a running horse
About as fast as a river flows after rain
About as slow as your nails grow
questions.why: The article says the plates move about as slowly as your fingernails grow.

wrong.A: Plates move far more slowly than a car.
wrong.B: Plates do not move as fast as a horse.
wrong.C: A river is much faster than the plates.

questions.stem: The article says rock folds up "like a rug that you push on the floor." What does fold mean here?
options: Bend and bunch up
Break into dust
Melt into a liquid
Sink under the sea
questions.why: A rug pushed on the floor bends and bunches up, and that is what the rock does when it folds.

wrong.B: The rock bends; it does not turn into dust.
wrong.C: Melting is how lava forms, not how rock folds.
wrong.D: Folded rock rises up instead of sinking.

questions.stem: What happens when two plates push hard on each other?
options: The ground gets flat
Lava turns into ice
The rock folds up and tall peaks slowly rise
The two plates stop moving and then never move again
questions.why: The article says the rock bends and folds up, and over a long time tall peaks rise.

wrong.A: The pushing makes the land rise, not get flat.
wrong.B: Lava does not turn into ice in the article.
wrong.D: The article says the plates keep moving.

questions.stem: How does a volcano grow?
options: Snow piles up on it
Lava cools, gets hard, and more lava piles on top
Rain washes rock onto it
Plates fold it like a rug and then flatten it again
questions.why: The article says lava cools and hardens, then more lava comes on top, building the volcano bit by bit.

wrong.A: Snow does not build a volcano.
wrong.C: Rain wears rock down; it does not build volcanoes.
wrong.D: Folding is a different way mountains grow.

questions.stem: Why does the article say mountains grow AND shrink?
options: Because plates and lava build them up while rain, wind, and ice wear them down
Because mountains melt every summer
Because people dig them away
Because they sink back into the sea each night
questions.why: The article shows forces that build mountains up and forces that slowly break them down.

wrong.B: Mountains do not melt every summer.
wrong.C: The article does not say people dig mountains away.
wrong.D: Mountains do not sink each night.

questions.stem: What can you infer about the mountains in Saudi Arabia by the Red Sea?
options: They were all built by people with big machines very long ago
They are made only of ice
They formed because moving land pushed and split the ground
They are taller than Mount Everest
questions.why: The article says they rose as the land by the Red Sea split apart, so moving land helped make them.

wrong.A: People did not build these mountains.
wrong.B: They are made of rock, not ice.
wrong.D: The article says Everest is the tallest mountain in the world.

questions.stem: How does the article explain the two ways mountains grow?
options: It tells a story about one climber
It lists the tallest mountains in order
It gives facts against volcanoes
It describes one way (folding) and then a different way (lava)
questions.why: The article first explains folding plates, then says some mountains grow in a different way, with lava.

wrong.A: There is no story about a climber.
wrong.B: The article only names Everest, not a list.
wrong.C: The article explains volcanoes; it does not argue against them.

LOW.prompt: Explain two ways that mountains can grow. Use facts and words from the article.
checklist: I explained two different ways mountains grow.
I used at least two key words from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: One way mountains grow is when two plates of the Earth's crust collide and push the rock between them up into folds. Another way is when hot melted rock called lava pours out onto the surface and hardens, and layer by layer this builds up into a volcano. Both ways take a very long time to make a tall mountain.

keyWords.example: The two bumper cars collide in the middle of the floor.

keyWords.definition: the very top of a mountain
keyWords.example: The hikers took a photo when they reached the summit.

keyWords.definition: the remains or marks of very old living things kept in rock
keyWords.example: The museum shows fossils of fish that lived long ago.

keyWords.definition: melted rock while it is still deep underground
keyWords.example: Magma can stay underground for a long time before it erupts.

keyWords.definition: the slow wearing away of rock or soil by water, wind, or ice
keyWords.example: Erosion from the waves has made the cliff smaller.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea?
options: Everest is the hardest mountain to climb.
Moving plates and volcanoes build mountains, while erosion slowly wears them down.
Fossils can be found anywhere on Earth.
Lava is hotter than magma.
questions.why: The article explains both how mountains grow (colliding plates, volcanoes) and how erosion wears them down.

wrong.A: The article does not compare how hard mountains are to climb.
wrong.C: Fossils are one detail about Everest.
wrong.D: The article does not compare how hot lava and magma are.

questions.stem: How did Mount Everest form, according to the article?
options: Lava cooled into hard layers over and over again
Ice pushed the rock upward
The plate carrying India crashed into Asia
Wind piled up sand into a tall hill
questions.why: The article says Everest formed when the plate carrying India crashed into Asia.

wrong.A: Layers of lava build volcanoes, not Everest.
wrong.B: Ice wears mountains down; it does not push them up.
wrong.D: Wind is part of erosion, which wears rock away.

questions.stem: What is the difference between magma and lava?
options: Magma is under the ground; lava is the same melted rock once it pours out at the surface
Magma is cold and lava is hot
Magma is a kind of ice
There is no difference at all between them
questions.why: The article says melted rock underground is magma, and when it pours out at the surface it is called lava.

wrong.B: Both are melted rock, so both are hot.
wrong.C: Magma is melted rock, not ice.
wrong.D: The article gives them different names for different places.

questions.stem: Climbers found fossils of sea animals near the top of Everest. What does this show?
options: Sea animals once climbed the mountain
The rock there was once under the sea
The summit is covered in water
Fossils fall from the sky
questions.why: The article says the fossils show that this rock was once under the sea before it was pushed up.

wrong.C: The summit is covered in snow, not water.
wrong.D: Fossils form in rock; they do not fall from the sky.

questions.stem: Which word from the article means "the slow breaking and carrying away of rock"?
options: Summit
Magma
Collide
Erosion
questions.why: The article says rain, wind, and ice break rock apart and carry it away, which is called erosion.

wrong.A: Summit is the top of a mountain.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare the crust to the shell of an egg?
options: To show that the crust is soft and wet
To show that the whole Earth is shaped exactly like a giant bird's egg in a nest
To help readers picture a hard outer layer that is cracked into pieces
To explain where eggs come from
questions.why: An egg shell is a thin, hard outer layer that can crack, which helps readers picture the crust and its plates.

wrong.A: The crust is described as hard, not soft.
wrong.B: The comparison is about the shell, not the Earth's shape.
wrong.D: The article is about mountains, not eggs.

questions.stem: Everest is still rising a few millimeters each year. What is the most likely reason?
options: The plates under it are still pushing together
Snow keeps piling up on the summit
Climbers keep leaving rocks and flags at the top
Erosion makes mountains taller
questions.why: Everest grew because plates collided, so if it is still rising, the plates must still be pushing.

wrong.B: Snow is not given as the reason it grows.
wrong.C: Climbers do not make the mountain grow.
wrong.D: Erosion wears mountains down, not up.

questions.stem: In what order does a volcano grow?
options: Lava cools first, then magma melts, then rock folds
Rock melts into magma, it pours out as lava, the lava hardens, and more layers pile on
Plates collide first, then fossils form in the rock, and then lava flows down the sides
Erosion starts, then the volcano rises
questions.why: The article says rock melts into magma, pours out as lava, cools and hardens, and then more lava flows on top.

wrong.A: This order is mixed up, and folding is a different process.
wrong.C: Fossils are not part of how a volcano grows.
wrong.D: Erosion wears mountains down; it does not start volcano growth.

MID.prompt: Mount Everest is growing taller, but erosion is also wearing it down. Explain both processes using details from the article.
checklist: I explained why Everest is still rising.
I explained what erosion does to mountains.
I used at least three key words from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: Mount Everest is still rising because the plate carrying India continues to collide with the plate carrying Asia, slowly pushing its summit a few millimeters higher every year. We know this mountain was once under the sea because climbers have found fossils of sea animals near its very top. At the same time, erosion from rain, wind, and ice is constantly wearing the mountain down, breaking rock apart and carrying it away, so the mountain's height is really a balance between these two opposite forces.

keyWords.definition: having to do with the huge moving plates of the Earth's crust
keyWords.example: Earthquakes often happen where tectonic plates meet.

keyWords.definition: to press something together so it takes up less space
keyWords.example: We had to compress the clothes to close the suitcase.

keyWords.definition: the slow raising of land to a higher level
keyWords.example: Uplift over thousands of years turned the seabed into a hill.

keyWords.definition: sand, mud, and bits of rock that settle in layers, often under water
keyWords.example: Sediment settled at the bottom of the jar of muddy water.

keyWords.definition: a long crack or split where land pulls apart
keyWords.example: Over time, the rift in the valley grew wider.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the article?
options: Mountains form only from volcanoes.
Mountains are shaped by tectonic forces and volcanoes that build them up and by erosion that wears them down.
Saudi Arabia has the highest mountains in the world.
Erosion stops mountains from forming.
questions.why: The article explains plate collisions, volcanoes, and erosion, showing that mountains are built up and worn down.

wrong.A: The article also explains mountains formed by colliding plates.
wrong.C: Everest, not a Saudi peak, is the highest.
wrong.D: Erosion wears mountains down but does not stop them forming.

questions.stem: According to the article, how did the Sarawat Mountains form?
options: They were uplifted along a rift as the Arabian Plate pulled away from Africa
Lava from one volcano piled into a single peak
The plate carrying India crashed into the Arabian Peninsula many millions of years ago
Sediment blew in from the desert
questions.why: The article says they were lifted along a rift as the Arabian Plate separated from Africa, which opened the Red Sea.

wrong.B: The article does not describe the Sarawat as one volcano.
wrong.C: India's plate crashed into Asia to form Everest.
wrong.D: Wind-blown sediment is not how the article says they formed.

questions.stem: What does it mean when colliding plates "compress" rock?
options: They heat the rock up until it melts and turns into magma
They wash it away
They squeeze it together so it bends and folds
They freeze it into ice
questions.why: Compress means to press together; the squeezed rock bends and folds upward.

wrong.A: Melting is how magma forms, not what compress means.
wrong.D: The article does not say the rock freezes.

questions.stem: Why do sea fossils near the top of Everest show that the rock began as sediment under an ocean?
options: Because sea creatures can live high on mountains
Because the fossils were carried up by climbers
Because rain brings fossils down from the sky
Because sea animals were buried in sediment on the sea floor, and uplift later raised that rock
questions.why: Sea animals live and are buried in the ocean, so the rock holding them must have formed there and been raised later.

wrong.A: Sea creatures cannot live on mountain tops.
wrong.B: The fossils are in the rock itself.
wrong.C: Fossils do not fall with rain.

questions.stem: How is the growth of a volcano different from the growth of Everest?
options: A volcano grows as layers of lava pile up, while Everest grows as colliding plates fold rock upward
A volcano grows by erosion, while Everest grows by rain
Both grow only when climbers reach the summit
A volcano grows faster because it is made of ice
questions.why: The article explains that volcanoes grow layer by layer from lava, while Everest rose from compressed, folded rock.

wrong.B: Erosion and rain wear mountains down.
wrong.C: Climbers do not make mountains grow.
wrong.D: Volcanoes are made of hardened lava, not ice.

questions.stem: What effect does erosion have on mountains?
options: It pushes plates together
It breaks rock apart and carries it away, wearing mountains down
It creates magma deep underground
It adds new fossils of sea creatures to the summit of the mountain each year
questions.why: The article says rain, wind, and ice break rock apart and carry the pieces away, so mountains wear down.

wrong.A: Plates move because of forces inside the Earth, not erosion.
wrong.D: Fossils were in the rock long before erosion.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe mountains as being "like living things"?
options: To argue that mountains breathe
To show that mountains have plants on them
To show that mountains change over time, growing and wearing down
To compare mountains to the many animals that live and climb on them
questions.why: Living things grow and age; the comparison shows that mountains also grow and are worn down over time.

wrong.A: The author does not claim mountains breathe.
wrong.B: Plants on mountains are not discussed.
wrong.D: The comparison is about change, not climbing animals.

questions.stem: Jabal Sawda keeps cool air even when the lowlands are hot. What can you infer?
options: Erosion makes the air cooler
The Red Sea freezes in winter and sends cold air up the slopes
Volcanoes make cold air
Higher places on a mountain are usually cooler than low land
questions.why: The article links Jabal Sawda's height of about three thousand meters to its cool air, so higher places tend to be cooler.

wrong.A: Erosion is not connected to the cool air.
wrong.B: The article does not say the Red Sea freezes.
wrong.C: Volcanoes are linked to heat, not cold air.

HIGH.prompt: Write a short explanation for a younger student of how the Sarawat Mountains or Mount Everest formed. Use the words tectonic, uplift, and either rift or compress.
checklist: I explained the steps of how the mountains formed in order.
I used at least three key words correctly.
I wrote clearly enough for a younger student to understand.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Mountains like the Sarawat Mountains or Mount Everest form because giant tectonic plates making up Earth's crust are always moving, just very slowly. When two plates collide, they compress the rock between them, folding and pushing it upward in a process called uplift that can take millions of years to build a tall mountain. The Sarawat Mountains formed differently, through a rift, where a piece of land slowly tore away from Africa and rose up beside the Red Sea. Either way, it is the slow movement of tectonic plates that ultimately uplifts the rock into the mountains we see today.
